extracted.intended_audience: readers and scholars of early 19th-century exploration, historical geography, and biography (readers of Park's life)
extracted.subtask_description: An editorial/appendix discussion evaluating historical claims about African geography (the Niger, Tombuctoo, Congo) and an argument about the social effects of Scottish education, drawing on traveller reports, ancient authorities, and empirical instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use practical instances to support social-historical claims
rubrics_metrics.description: “The truth of this remark will be apparent from a few practical instances, drawn from the experience of common life, of that general superiority which is here attributed to the lower classes of the Scotch, as the effect of their superior industry and intelligence...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support broad causal claims (e.g., education -> social improvement) with concrete, representative examples: occupational mobility (gardeners, stewards, clerks), prevalence of non-commissioned officers raised from the ranks, statistical summaries (Mr. Martin's beggar survey), and anecdotal evidence (ransoms paid for Scottish prisoners). Use such instances to illustrate mechanisms (industry, frugality, foresight) and expected outcomes (reduced crime, social mobility).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer first-hand, authenticated testimony over hearsay
rubrics_metrics.description: “Mr. Jackson derived his whole knowledge of Tombuctoo from the accounts of native traders; upon whose unsupported testimony very little reliance can be placed; especially as to matters of detail, or such facts as require to be stated with any degree of exactness.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing accounts of distant places, prioritize direct observation and authenticated documents (journals, expedition reports) and treat second-hand trader reports or long‑removed hearsay with skepticism, especially for precise details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give weight to ancient authorities when their methods fit the question
rubrics_metrics.description: “The principal ground of this supposition is, the opinion of some of the best informed writers of antiquity... since there is good reason to believe, that the knowledge of the ancients concerning the interior of Africa was much more extensive and accurate than that of the moderns. It is justly observed by Dr. Robertson, that the geographical discoveries of the ancients were made chiefly by land, those of the moderns by sea...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the provenance and methods of sources: ancient land-based geographic knowledge can be especially relevant for interior features. Do not dismiss antiquity outright; assess whether their mode of inquiry (land travel, local intelligence) is appropriate to the question at hand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test geographic hypotheses against physical plausibility (volume/terminus/levels)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Against the hypothesis of an inland termination of the Niger, several objections have been urged, which are well deserving of attention. They are principally founded on a consideration of the vast magnitude which the Niger must have attained... and the difficulty of conceiving so prodigious a stream to be discharged into lakes, and evaporated even by an African sun.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate river-identity hypotheses by physical constraints: estimated discharge, expected behavior over long courses, plausibility of evaporation/inland loss, and whether an inland terminus can account for the river's observed magnitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use topographic/level comparisons as decisive constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: “The principal, and apparently decisive, objection against this supposed junction of the Niger and the Nile, is grounded upon a comparison of the great difference of level between the beds of the two rivers.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantitative differences in elevation and gradient between proposed connected waterways can decisively confirm or refute identifications; incorporate known altitudes and distances into the argument rather than relying solely on direction or hearsay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroborate hypotheses with multiple independent observations (navigators, traders, soundings)
rubrics_metrics.description: “There are other testimonies to the magnitude of the Congo... Captain Scobell ... the Congo is described as 'an immense river'... accounts state, that the waters of the Congo may be distinguished at sea more than thirty leagues from the coast, and that the water is fresh at the distance of thirty miles.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assemble corroborative evidence from independent observers (naval officers, traders, charts, soundings) about features such as breadth, current, floating islands, and freshwater extent to strengthen claims about a river's magnitude and course.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess seasonal behaviour and flood regularity as evidence of origin/character
rubrics_metrics.description: “All the accounts concur in representing, that the stream of the Congo is of a more uniform height, and subject to much less variation from the dry and rainy seasons... it may be considered to be in a perpetual state of flood.... the difference between the highest point of the Congo about February, and the lowest in September, is only about nine feet...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use observed seasonal amplitude and flood patterns (magnitude of rise/fall) to infer basin characteristics and to compare rivers; markedly different seasonal regimes argue against simple identity of two rivers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid relying on etymological/name resemblances as primary evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: “Arguments founded upon etymological conjectures, supposed resemblances of names, or affinity of languages, &c. &c., are, for the most part, too arbitrary and fanciful, and liable to too much uncertainty…”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat name similarities and etymological conjectures as suggestive at best; they should not substitute for physical, topographic, or direct observational evidence in geographic identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value well-documented company/mission journals as authentic sources
rubrics_metrics.description: “The editor has been favoured by Mr. Macaulay ... with a sight of the Journals of the expedition to Teembo ... They do great credit to the writers (especially the Journal to Teembo) and contain many valuable and interesting particulars; several of which have been given to the public in the Reports of the Sierra Leone Company...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expedition and company reports (Sierra Leone Company, African Association) and their journals are important primary sources; compile, select, and publish material from them to improve public and scholarly knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer schemes of exploration that maximize ease and safety
rubrics_metrics.description: “But, whether the Congo be the outlet of the Niger or not, it certainly offers the best opening for exploring the interior of Africa of any scheme that has ever yet been attempted; and the ease and safety with which it might be conducted, needs no comment.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing exploratory routes, prioritize practical considerations—ease of access, navigability, safety for personnel—alongside scientific aims; feasibility can determine whether an expedition is undertaken or succeeds.

rubrics_metrics.name: When multiple causes exist, argue for primacy with comparative reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is true that there are several other circumstances, besides the system of public education in Scotland, which have assisted in producing that extraordinary change of national character... But of the various causes which have contributed to this change, education is by far the most important...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge multiple contributing factors for a historical phenomenon but present comparative evidence and reasoning to justify why one cause (education) should be regarded as primary, using observable outcomes and mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use statistical and survey data to support social claims
rubrics_metrics.description: “From the statement which Mr. Martin prepared ... of 2000 beggars, whose cases were investigated by Mr. Martin, the following is a summary. ... Irish 679; Scotch 65; Foreign 30.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include quantified surveys and tabulated data (even simple tallies) to substantiate comparative social claims (e.g., prevalence of mendicity among groups); such figures bolster arguments about social effects and differences.
